- Without `.autoDispose`, the provider is kept forever; this is fine for app-wide singletons (the auth notifier, an analytics client).

questions.question: How does Riverpod code generation (riverpod_generator) work?
questions.answer:
riverpod\_generator is a build\_runner code-gen layer over flutter\_riverpod. You annotate functions or classes with @riverpod and the generator emits the matching provider declaration. It's optional, and it is how the Riverpod documentation presents the library now.

### What it does
- `@riverpod String greeting(Ref ref) => 'hi'` → generates `greetingProvider`
- Function with parameters becomes a family automatically — no `.family` boilerplate
- A class annotated with `@riverpod` becomes a Notifier/AsyncNotifier; methods you add are public mutators
- `@Riverpod(keepAlive: true)` makes it non-autoDispose; default is autoDispose
- Older generated code took a per-provider ref type (`GreetingRef`, `ProductRef`); current versions take a plain `Ref`, so a codebase full of `XxxRef` parameters is due a regeneration

### Why use it
- Eliminates the boilerplate of choosing the right provider type — the generator picks Notifier/AsyncNotifier/Stream from your return type
- **Refactor-safe** — rename a function and the generated provider name follows
- Encourages best practices (autoDispose by default, family inferred from args)

Setup: add `riverpod_generator` and `build_runner` to dev\_dependencies, then `dart run build_runner watch -d`.

questions.question: When should you pick Notifier vs AsyncNotifier vs StateProvider?
questions.answer:
All three hold mutable state, so choose by how it is created: a bare value, synchronous logic, or an async load whose loading and error phases consumers have to render.

### StateProvider\<T>
- **Trivial mutable values** — a search string, a checkbox, a tab index
- Direct setter via `ref.read(p.notifier).state = newValue`
- No place to put logic; if you need any, you've outgrown StateProvider — move to Notifier

### Notifier\<T> (sync)
- Synchronous, in-memory state with logic — a cart, a filter set, a wizard step
- Methods on the class become the mutators (`add`, `remove`, `next`)
- `build()` returns T directly — no AsyncValue wrapping
- Use when state isn't loaded from IO

### AsyncNotifier\<T> (async)
- State is loaded asynchronously and consumers should see loading/error/data
- `build()` returns Future\<T>; the provider's value is `AsyncValue<T>`
- Mutators typically wrap `AsyncValue.guard(() async {...})` to keep the type safe
- Use for any state hydrated from an API/DB and updated by user actions

Rule of thumb: start with the simplest. StateProvider for plain values, Notifier for synchronous logic, AsyncNotifier the moment IO is involved.

questions.question: How do you control rebuilds with select() and Equatable-style equality?
questions.answer:
By default, watching a provider rebuilds the consumer on ANY change to the state. For coarse state (a big User object, a list, a settings bag) that's wasteful — most fields don't matter to a given widget.

Two levers:

- `ref.watch(provider.select((s) => s.field))`:
- Computes a derived value and only rebuilds when THAT changes (by ==)
- Works on any provider whose state is a value type with stable equality
- **On AsyncValue**: `provider.select((s) => s.valueOrNull?.field)` — handle null/loading explicitly

- Stable equality on your state:
- Plain Dart classes use identity equality — every rebuild creates a new instance, every selector "changes"
- Override `==` and `hashCode`, or use `freezed` / `equatable` — the state class becomes value-typed
- Lists/Maps are still by reference — wrap them in BuiltValue or store as IList/IMap (fast\_immutable\_collections) for content equality

When .select isn't enough: split your provider. A coarse provider with many unrelated fields is a code smell — break it into focused providers and let watchers pick exactly the one they care about.

questions.question: How do ProviderScope overrides work — at app start vs at runtime?
questions.answer:
Overrides replace a provider's implementation within a scope. The scope is the ProviderContainer (in tests / pure Dart) or the nearest ProviderScope ancestor (in widgets). Overrides are how you inject mocks for tests, how you swap an implementation per environment, and how you scope state to a subtree.

### Flavors of override
- `overrideWithValue(value)` — replaces the produced value with a constant
- `overrideWith((ref) => ...)` — replaces the provider's build with a different builder; the only option for Notifier/AsyncNotifier providers
- **Keep the shape** — a `Provider<ApiClient>` is overridden with another builder producing an ApiClient; type mismatches are compile errors

### App-start vs runtime
- **At app start**: pass `overrides:` to the root ProviderScope. This is how you inject the env config, the dependency graph for the chosen flavor, or test-only fakes
- **At runtime / per-subtree**: nest a ProviderScope deeper in the widget tree. Children use the overridden version; everything outside still sees the parent's. Useful for multi-tenant or sandboxed sub-apps
- Switching at runtime by remounting the ProviderScope with a new key forces a clean reset of all autoDispose providers

Gotcha: overriding a provider at the root affects every dependent. If you override only at a child scope, providers UP the dependency chain are NOT recomputed under the override unless they themselves are also overridden.

questions.question: How do you fire side effects (navigation, snackbars, dialogs) from Riverpod state?
questions.answer:
Side effects must run once per state transition, but `build()` can run many times for the same state — so navigation, snackbars and dialogs never belong inside it. Riverpod gives you `ref.listen` for exactly this: subscribe to changes, run an imperative effect, do not rebuild the widget.

### Pattern
- Use `ref.listen` inside `build()` — it's safe to call there because it doesn't make build dependent on the value
- The callback receives `(previous, next)` — branch on transitions, not on snapshots
- For one-shot success/error states, model them as a transient `AsyncValue<Result>` and react to the new error/data — clear the state afterwards if you want to allow re-trigger
- In a Notifier, prefer not to call Navigator from inside the notifier itself — it makes the notifier coupled to the widget tree. Surface a state and let a widget react to it.

For app-wide effects (deep links, push notifications), expose a stream from a provider and let a top-level ConsumerWidget listen on it.

questions.question: Pull-to-refresh wipes your list and flashes a spinner before the new data lands. What causes that, and how do you keep the old rows on screen?
questions.answer:
The flash happens because something threw the previous value away — an AsyncValue can carry the old data through a reload, and assigning a bare `AsyncLoading` is what discards it.

Three ways to trigger a reload, and they are not interchangeable:
- `ref.invalidate(p)` — marks the provider dirty and disposes its state; the rebuild happens lazily, the next time anyone reads it. Fire-and-forget, safe to call twice in a row.
- `ref.refresh(p)` — the same invalidation, but it reads the provider back immediately and returns the new value. `ref.refresh(p.future)` gives you a Future to await.
- `ref.invalidateSelf()` — the same thing from inside a Notifier, after a mutation that changed the server state.

What the consumer actually sees while `build()` re-runs:
- The state is an `AsyncLoading` that still carries the previous data. `isLoading` and `isRefreshing` are both true, and `valueOrNull` still returns the old list.
- `when()` skips its loading branch on a refresh by default (`skipLoadingOnRefresh: true`), so the old rows stay put. It does NOT skip it when the rebuild was caused by a changed dependency — that is `skipLoadingOnReload`, which defaults to false.
- Writing `state = const AsyncLoading()` by hand in a mutator drops the previous value, and that is your spinner flash. Assign the result of `AsyncValue.guard` directly, or use `AsyncLoading<T>().copyWithPrevious(state)` when you want an explicit in-flight flag without losing the data.

For the RefreshIndicator itself, return the provider's future from `onRefresh` so the spinner lives exactly as long as the fetch, not one frame longer.

questions.question: A provider needs data from two other async providers before it can compute anything. How do you write it without nesting when() calls?
questions.answer:
Have the derived provider await the sources' futures instead of pattern-matching two AsyncValues against each other.

Every async provider exposes two things you can watch:
- `ref.watch(p)` gives `AsyncValue<T>` — the right shape for a widget, which has to render loading and error states.
- `ref.watch(p.future)` gives `Future<T>` — the right shape for another provider, because you can just await it.

Inside a `FutureProvider` or an `AsyncNotifier.build()`, watching `.future` still registers the dependency, so the derived provider re-runs whenever either source changes. Errors need no plumbing either: an await rethrows, the exception escapes `build()`, and Riverpod turns it into `AsyncError` for you with the original stack trace.

### Rules that keep it correct
- Use `Future.wait` when the two loads are independent, sequential awaits when the second needs the first's result.
- Never `ref.read(p.future)` here — a read does not subscribe, so the derived provider silently goes stale when the source updates.
- Keep `.future` out of widgets. A widget that awaits has nothing to show meanwhile; watch the AsyncValue there and let `when` do the branching.
- The widget ends up with one AsyncValue to render instead of two, which is the whole point.

questions.question: Your AsyncNotifier awaits a slow request and then touches ref; the user pops the screen mid-flight. What breaks, and how do you write it safely?
questions.answer:
The provider is disposed the moment its last listener goes away, so the code that resumes after the await is running on a dead Ref and throws instead of quietly doing nothing.

### What actually happens
- An autoDispose provider (the default with code generation) is disposed as soon as the screen that watched it is popped.
- Riverpod does not cancel your Future — Dart has no cancellation. The HTTP call keeps running and its `then` still fires.
- Touching `ref.read` / `ref.watch`, or assigning `state`, after disposal throws a StateError. `AsyncValue.guard` does not save you: it wraps the call, not the assignment that follows.

### How to write it safely
- Check `ref.mounted` after every await before touching ref or state, and return early when it is false.
- Register the real cancellation in `ref.onDispose` — cancel the Dio CancelToken, close the client, cancel timers and stream subscriptions. That turns an abandoned request into a cheap one instead of a leak.
- When the work genuinely must survive navigation (an upload, a payment confirmation), take `ref.keepAlive()` at the start and close the returned link in a `finally`, so the provider is disposable again once the work lands.
- Do not paper over it by dropping autoDispose everywhere — you trade a crash for an unbounded cache and stale screens.

The widget side has the same shape with a different guard: after an await in a callback, check the widget's own `mounted` before using `context`.

questions.question: What are the key security best practices for Flutter mobile apps?
questions.answer:
Mobile security splits into five layers, and an interviewer usually wants one concrete control named per layer.

### Data at rest
- flutter\_secure\_storage for tokens and keys — Keychain on iOS, Keystore-backed storage on Android
- SQLCipher, or an encrypted Hive/Isar box, when a local database holds sensitive rows
- **Never SharedPreferences for secrets** — it is a plain XML/plist file, readable on a rooted device

### Data in transit
- HTTPS everywhere, enforced by App Transport Security on iOS and Network Security Config on Android
- Certificate or public-key pinning for high-value APIs, always with a backup pin
- Never disable certificate validation, not even behind a debug flag you might ship

### Code and binary
- Build releases with `--obfuscate --split-debug-info`, and archive the symbol files per version
- **No hardcoded secrets** — a key compiled into the binary is a published key. Keep it server-side and proxy the call.
- Strip token, request-body and PII logging from release builds

### Authentication and session
- Short-lived access tokens plus rotating refresh tokens
- OAuth through the system browser with PKCE, never a WebView
- Biometrics (local\_auth) as a convenience unlock over a real credential, not as the credential
- **Device signals** — root/jailbreak, Play Integrity, App Attest — as input to a server-side risk decision, not as a client-side gate

### Standards to name
- OWASP Mobile Top 10 (2024 revision) opens with M1 Improper Credential Usage, M2 Inadequate Supply Chain Security, M3 Insecure Authentication/Authorization, M4 Insufficient Input/Output Validation, M5 Insecure Communication
- OWASP MASVS is the requirements standard behind it — MASVS-STORAGE, CRYPTO, AUTH, NETWORK, PLATFORM, CODE, RESILIENCE, PRIVACY — and MASTG is the matching test guide. Naming MASVS instead of only the Top 10 is what separates a senior answer here.

questions.question: What is SSL/certificate pinning and how do you implement it in Flutter?
questions.answer:
Certificate pinning prevents Man-in-the-Middle (MITM) attacks by hardcoding the expected server certificate or public key in the app. Even if an attacker installs a custom CA, the app rejects their certificate.

### Two things you can pin
- **Certificate pinning** — pin the whole leaf certificate. Breaks on every renewal.
- Public key (SPKI) pinning — pin the SHA-256 of the public key. Survives renewals while the key is reused, which is why it is the usual choice.

### How to implement it in Flutter
- **Strongest**: build the HttpClient with a SecurityContext that trusts only your certificate — `SecurityContext(withTrustedRoots: false)..setTrustedCertificatesBytes(...)`. Anything else fails the handshake.
- **Platform level**: an Android `<pin-set>` in the network security config, or a pinning-capable native library. This also covers WebViews and any other HTTP client in the process.
- **Common but wrong**: doing the comparison in `badCertificateCallback`. That callback only fires when validation has ALREADY failed, so an attacker whose CA is installed in the system trust store never reaches it and your pinning is silently bypassed.

### Operational rules
- Ship a backup pin for the next key, or the first renewal takes every installed app offline
- Make the pin set updatable through signed remote config, and keep the pin valid longer than the oldest app version you still support
- Pin only hosts you control — pinning a third-party CDN hands them your uptime
- **Test the failure path**: with pinning on, an intercepting proxy such as Proxyman or Charles must fail

questions.question: How does OAuth 2.0 with PKCE work for mobile apps and why is it required?
questions.answer:
Public clients (mobile apps, SPAs) cannot keep a client\_secret confidential — the secret would be embedded in the app binary, trivially extracted. PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange, RFC 7636) replaces the client\_secret with a per-flow proof, so a stolen authorization code is useless without the matching verifier.

### The flow
1. App generates a random `code_verifier` (43–128 chars, URL-safe)
2. App computes `code_challenge = base64url(SHA256(code_verifier))`
3. App opens the auth URL with `code_challenge` \+ `code_challenge_method=S256`
4. User signs in; the IdP redirects back to the app with `code`
5. App exchanges the code at the token endpoint, sending the original `code_verifier`
6. The IdP recomputes SHA256(verifier), compares to the stored challenge, issues tokens only if they match

If an attacker intercepts the redirect URI (registered scheme hijack) and steals the code, they cannot exchange it because they don't know the verifier.

### Other requirements for mobile
- OAuth 2.1 folds PKCE in as mandatory for every client and drops the implicit grant; RFC 8252 (OAuth for Native Apps) says the same about the system browser. An IdP still offering implicit flow or a static secret to a mobile app is a finding, not a feature.
- Use the system browser (ASWebAuthenticationSession on iOS, Custom Tabs on Android) — never WebView. WebView can be inspected, drained for credentials, and triggers anti-phishing flags.
- Use claimed/universal links for the redirect URI when possible — survives OS updates and beats most scheme-hijack attacks.
- Bind tokens to the device when the IdP supports DPoP or mTLS.

questions.question: How does code obfuscation work in Flutter, and how do you symbolicate crashes after enabling it?
questions.answer:
Dart compiles to AOT machine code on release builds, which is harder to read than JS/Java but still leaks identifier names in the snapshot. `--obfuscate` strips those names; `--split-debug-info=<dir>` writes the symbol map to a separate file you keep server-side.

### What obfuscation does
- Replaces class, method, and field names with short opaque tokens in the binary
- Reduces the value of static analysis for an attacker reverse-engineering your APK/IPA
- Does NOT encrypt assets, does NOT prevent decompilation, does NOT secure secrets — pair with other defenses

### The symbol-map file
- Contains the mapping from obfuscated tokens back to your real symbols
- MUST be archived per release/version — it's the only way to make a future crash readable
- **Treat it like source**: keep it private, ideally in your CI artifact store

### Symbolicating crashes
- On a stack trace from an obfuscated build, frames look like `package:_oz/abc123.dart 15:7`
- Run `flutter symbolize -i <stacktrace.txt> -d <split-debug-info-dir>/app.android-arm64.symbols` to recover real names
- Crashlytics, Sentry, and similar uploaders accept the symbols file and symbolicate automatically — upload from CI on each release
questions.code_example:
# 1) Build a release with obfuscation + split debug info
flutter build apk --release \
  --obfuscate \
  --split-debug-info=build/symbols/v1_2_3

flutter build ipa --release \
  --obfuscate \
  --split-debug-info=build/symbols/v1_2_3

# 2) Archive the symbols by app version, e.g.
#    s3://acme-mobile/symbols/android/1.2.3/
#    s3://acme-mobile/symbols/ios/1.2.3/

# 3) Upload to your crash reporter (Crashlytics example)
firebase crashlytics:symbols:upload \
  --app=1:123:android:abc \
  build/symbols/v1_2_3

# 4) Symbolicate a stack trace by hand if needed
flutter symbolize \
  -i ./crash.txt \
  -d build/symbols/v1_2_3/app.android-arm64.symbols

# ── CI gate (GitHub Actions example) ─────────────────
# Fail the release pipeline if symbols aren't archived
# - run: |
#     test -f build/symbols/v${VER}/app.android-arm64.symbols
#     test -f build/symbols/v${VER}/app.ios-arm64.symbols
# - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
#   with:
#     name: symbols-v${VER}
#     path: build/symbols/v${VER}
#     retention-days: 365

questions.question: What are App Transport Security (iOS) and Network Security Config (Android), and when do you have to touch them?
questions.answer:
Both platforms ship a system-level network policy that runs BEFORE your code. They block plaintext HTTP, weak ciphers, and self-signed certs by default. They also let you opt in to stricter policies (HTTPS-only by domain, custom CAs, debug-only relaxations). If your traffic looks fine in dev but mysteriously breaks in production, this is the first place to look.

### iOS — App Transport Security (ATS)
- Configured in Info.plist under `NSAppTransportSecurity`
- Blocks HTTP, TLS < 1.2, and weak forward-secrecy ciphers by default
- Granular exceptions per domain via `NSExceptionDomains`
- Apple actively rejects apps that turn off ATS globally without justification
- Use `NSAllowsArbitraryLoadsInWebContent` if you specifically need cleartext WebView content but want strict native networking

### Android — Network Security Config
- XML at `res/xml/network_security_config.xml`, referenced from AndroidManifest with `android:networkSecurityConfig`
- `cleartextTrafficPermitted="false"` is the default on API 28+
- Define `<domain-config>` to whitelist self-signed certs for staging, or custom CAs for enterprise environments
- `<debug-overrides>` lets you accept user-installed CAs (Charles, Proxyman) for debug builds only — never in release

### When you must touch them
- Talking to a service that doesn't have proper TLS (legacy IoT, sensor) — narrow exception per domain
- Using a corporate root CA that the OS doesn't trust
- Debugging with a man-in-the-middle proxy in development
- Allowing cleartext during gradual TLS rollout

Never globally permit cleartext or arbitrary loads in production. Reviewers and security audits will flag it.
questions.code_example:
<!-- iOS: ios/Runner/Info.plist — narrow ATS exception per domain -->
<key>NSAppTransportSecurity</key>
<dict>
  <key>NSAllowsArbitraryLoads</key>
  <false/>
  <key>NSExceptionDomains</key>
  <dict>
    <key>legacy-sensor.example.com</key>
    <dict>
      <!-- Plaintext only for THIS host, only because we can't fix the device -->
      <key>NSExceptionAllowsInsecureHTTPLoads</key>
      <true/>
      <key>NSIncludesSubdomains</key>
      <false/>
    </dict>
  </dict>
</dict>

<!-- Android: android/app/src/main/res/xml/network_security_config.xml -->
<network-security-config>
  <!-- Default: HTTPS only, system-trusted CAs only -->
  <base-config cleartextTrafficPermitted="false">
    <trust-anchors>
      <certificates src="system"/>
    </trust-anchors>
  </base-config>

  <!-- Staging: pin a self-signed cert -->
  <domain-config>
    <domain includeSubdomains="true">staging.example.com</domain>
    <trust-anchors>
      <certificates src="@raw/staging_ca"/>
    </trust-anchors>
  </domain-config>

  <!-- Debug-only: accept proxy-installed CAs (Charles, Proxyman) -->
  <debug-overrides>
    <trust-anchors>
      <certificates src="system"/>
      <certificates src="user"/>
    </trust-anchors>
  </debug-overrides>
</network-security-config>

<!-- AndroidManifest.xml:
     <application
       android:networkSecurityConfig="@xml/network_security_config"
       ...> -->

questions.question: How do you avoid leaking sensitive data through logs, screenshots, and clipboard?
questions.answer:
Most production leaks are not fancy attacks — they are tokens in crash logs, PII in analytics events, and payment screens captured in the app switcher.

### Logs
- Never `print` or `debugPrint` tokens, refresh codes, or full request/response bodies in release. Configure a log filter that strips Authorization headers and known PII keys before reaching the sink.
- Crash reporters (Crashlytics, Sentry) capture device state — set scrubbing rules for keys like password, otp, ssn, card.
- Don't ship a debug log file to the user via share/email without redacting first.

### Screenshots / app switcher / screen recording
- **Android**: `WindowManager.FLAG_SECURE` blocks screenshots, screen recording, and the recents-thumbnail. Apply only on screens that need it (login, card entry, secret notes) — global FLAG\_SECURE breaks accessibility tools.
- **iOS**: there's no equivalent of FLAG\_SECURE. Standard practice is to overlay a blurred image when the app resigns active so the recents preview doesn't expose the screen.

### Clipboard
- iOS Universal Clipboard syncs across the user's devices — a secret copied on the phone lands on their Mac. Flutter's `Clipboard.setData` exposes no local-only or expiry option, so a secret you really must copy needs a small platform channel that sets the UIPasteboard item with `.localOnly` and an expiration date, plus a timer that clears it.
- **Android**: pre-13 the clipboard is readable by any foreground app. Same advice — don't copy secrets unless required, clear quickly.

### Keyboard
- `TextField` with `autocorrect: false, enableSuggestions: false` and `obscureText: true` for password-like fields prevents iOS/Android from caching content in their dictionaries.

questions.question: How do you implement a robust access-token + refresh-token rotation strategy?
questions.answer:
Long-lived bearer tokens are the most common credential-leak vector in mobile apps. The standard defense is short-lived access tokens (minutes) plus a refresh token that mints new ones — but the refresh path itself has subtle pitfalls.

### Design principles
- Access token in memory (or short-TTL secure storage). Refresh token in flutter\_secure\_storage. Never put either in SharedPreferences or in the URL.
- **Access token short** — 5–15 minutes. Refresh token longer (days/weeks) but EVERY refresh issues a NEW refresh token (rotation). The IdP invalidates the old one. If an attacker steals an old refresh token and uses it, the legitimate device gets a 401 on its next refresh — that's your detection signal.
- **Single-flight refresh**: under concurrent requests, multiple 401s shouldn't all kick off concurrent refreshes. Funnel them through one in-flight Future.
- On server-side revocation (logout, password change, suspicious activity): the IdP rejects the refresh token; the client must wipe credentials and force re-auth.
- Bind the refresh token to the device when possible — DPoP, mTLS, or device-attested certificates make a stolen token unusable on another device.

### Flow
1. Request returns 401
2. Acquire the refresh lock (single-flight) → call /refresh with the refresh token → receive new pair
3. Update storage atomically; release the lock; replay the original request
4. If /refresh returns 401: wipe storage, navigate to login

questions.question: What are the security pitfalls of using WebView in a Flutter app?
questions.answer:
WebViews host arbitrary web content with the trust of your app process. Everything you've protected with secure storage, certificate pinning, and platform sandboxing can be bypassed if you mis-configure a WebView. Several apps have shipped account-takeover bugs through WebViews.

Things to nail down:

- Don't load untrusted URLs at all. If the source isn't a domain you fully control, prefer the system browser (url\_launcher with `mode: LaunchMode.externalApplication`).

- Disable JavaScript bridges unless required. `JavaScriptChannel`s let web code call your Dart code. Treat any channel as a public API: validate inputs ruthlessly, allow only specific origins, and never expose anything that opens secure storage, the file system, or device APIs by name.

- Restrict navigation. Use `NavigationDelegate` (or onNavigationRequest) to block redirects to non-whitelisted hosts. Phishing pages love a forgotten redirect.

- **Cookies and storage**: WebViews share cookies with the app's WebKit/WebView session. Don't reuse the same web view for an in-app webview and an OAuth page — clear cookies between flows or use a session-only configuration.

- **Mixed content**: an HTTPS page must not pull HTTP subresources. Android's WebView defaults to MIXED\_CONTENT\_NEVER\_ALLOW on modern API levels, but plugins and copy-pasted setup code still switch it to COMPATIBILITY\_MODE — check what your app actually sets.

- **File access**: `setAllowFileAccess(false)` and `setAllowFileAccessFromFileURLs(false)` unless you specifically need them. file:// URLs in a WebView can read app sandbox files.

- Don't put auth in WebView. OAuth/OIDC flows must use the system browser (ASWebAuthenticationSession / Custom Tabs), not an embedded WebView. Apple actively rejects apps that put their sign-in into a WebView.

- Keep the WebView engine up to date. On Android, system WebView is updated by Google Play; you still need to test against the version range your install base runs.

questions.question: Why is a deep link untrusted input, and what stops another app from stealing yours?
questions.answer:
A deep link arrives from outside your process, unauthenticated, with attacker-controlled parameters, and a plain custom scheme has no owner — any app on the device can register `myapp://` too.

### Claim your links properly
- **Android App Links** — `android:autoVerify="true"` on the intent filter plus `/.well-known/assetlinks.json` served over HTTPS from the domain, listing your package name and the SHA-256 fingerprint of the signing certificate. Verification is done by the system against your server, so no other app can claim the same https link.
- **iOS Universal Links** — an `apple-app-site-association` file on the domain naming your Team ID and bundle ID, plus the Associated Domains entitlement in the app.
- A custom scheme has none of that. On Android the user gets a chooser, on iOS the winner is undefined. Never return an OAuth code, a session token or a password-reset token over a bare scheme; use a claimed https link, and PKCE so an intercepted code is useless.

### Then treat the payload as hostile
- Allowlist routes. Map the incoming path to a known route table and send anything unrecognised to a 404 screen — never build a screen or a query straight from link text.
- Never open a WebView with a URL taken from the link. That is an open redirect and a ready-made phishing page inside your app's chrome.
- Never let a link perform a privileged action on arrival — deleting an account, confirming a payment, marking an email verified. A link navigates; the destination re-checks the session and asks for confirmation.
- Parameters are not authorization. `?userId=42` identifies a screen, never a user; the server decides what the caller may see.
- Attribution SDKs deliver deferred deep links from a third-party server — same rules apply.

Test the failure paths: `adb shell am start -a android.intent.action.VIEW -d '...'` and `xcrun simctl openurl booted '...'` let you fire hostile links by hand, and a second app declaring the same scheme proves whether your links are actually verified.

questions.question: A teammate wants to add a pub package with 30 likes to handle payments. How do you decide, and how do you keep the dependency tree safe over time?
questions.answer:
Every package you add runs inside your app with your app's permissions, and so does everything it depends on — which is why OWASP lists supply chain as its own top-ten category.

### What to check before adding one
- **Maintenance signals over popularity**: recent commits, issues triaged, a changelog, a verified publisher, and whether it is pinned to an SDK version you can move off later.
- Does it ship native code? An `android/` or `ios/` folder means Kotlin, Swift or C running outside the Dart sandbox, plus its own Gradle and CocoaPods dependencies that never show up in the pub graph.
- What does it need to work? A package that wants INTERNET, contacts, or accessibility for a job that does not obviously require them is the whole attack.
- Size of the transitive tree — `flutter pub deps` shows what you are really installing.
- Licence, and whether you could fork and maintain the thing yourself if it is abandoned. For something as sensitive as payments, prefer the vendor's official SDK or a thin wrapper you own.

### Keeping it safe afterwards
- Commit `pubspec.lock` for applications. That file, not the caret range in pubspec.yaml, is what ships.
- Automate upgrades with Dependabot or Renovate so bumps arrive as reviewable PRs instead of a yearly big-bang.
- Treat dev\_dependencies as production risk. build\_runner and every code generator execute arbitrary code on the CI machine that holds your signing keys.
- Run a secret scanner and a licence check in CI, and re-run `flutter pub outdated` on a schedule so you learn about a security release before an auditor does.
- Avoid `dependency_overrides` outside a short-lived fix, and never publish a package that carries one.
questions.code_example:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

# What is actually being installed, including the transitive tree
flutter pub deps --style=compact
flutter pub outdated --show-all

# Does the package ship native code that runs outside the Dart sandbox?
find "$(flutter pub cache list --json >/dev/null 2>&1; echo ~/.pub-cache/hosted)" \
  -maxdepth 4 -type d \( -name android -o -name ios \) | head

# ── CI gate: the lockfile that ships must be the one in git ──────────
flutter pub get
if ! git diff --quiet -- pubspec.lock; then
  echo "pubspec.lock changed during CI — commit the resolved lockfile" >&2
  exit 1
fi

# ── CI gate: no secrets, no forbidden licences ──────────────────────
gitleaks detect --no-banner --redact
dart run license_checker check-licenses --config license_config.yaml

# Reproduce a build from the lockfile only (no silent resolution drift)
flutter pub get --enforce-lockfile
flutter build appbundle --release \
  --obfuscate --split-debug-info=build/symbols

questions.question: local_auth returns true after a Face ID prompt. What has that actually proven, and how do you turn it into real protection?
questions.answer:
It proves only that the operating system was willing to say yes on this device, in your process, right now — it is a UI gate, not a credential.

### What the check does not give you
- No proof to your backend. The result never leaves the device, so a server that accepts a "biometrics passed" flag from the client is accepting an attacker's flag too.
- No resistance to a patched binary. The branch that reads the boolean is in your code; on a rooted or repackaged app it can simply be flipped.
- No idea who is in front of the camera beyond "someone enrolled on this device", and the passcode fallback widens that to anyone who knows the PIN.

How to make it mean something — bind data to the biometric instead of branching on a boolean:
- Keep the refresh token in the Keychain with an access control that requires biometry, or in an Android Keystore key created with user authentication required. The ciphertext is then undecryptable without a fresh match, so skipping the prompt gets you nothing.
- Invalidate on enrollment change. The Keychain flag for the current biometry set and the Android equivalent both destroy the key when a new face or finger is enrolled — that is the control that stops someone adding their own fingerprint to an unlocked device.
- Handle the real error cases explicitly: no hardware, nothing enrolled, biometry locked out after repeated failures, and permission denied. Each one needs a different path, and the fallback has to be a real credential, not a bypass.
- Re-prompt for high-value actions and re-lock after a background timeout instead of unlocking the session forever.

The mental model an interviewer wants: biometrics unlock a secret that the server already trusts. They never replace the server's own check.

questions.question: A third-party service hands you an API key and says to put it in the app. What do you do with it?
questions.answer:
Start by classifying it, because anything the app can read at runtime an attacker with the binary can read too.

There are two kinds of key, and only one of them can ship:
- **Publishable identifiers** — the Firebase config, a Maps key, an analytics or purchases public key. These are meant to be visible; they are protected by server-side restrictions, not by secrecy. Lock them to your bundle id and signing fingerprint, add referrer or platform restrictions, quota caps, and Firebase App Check or the equivalent attestation.
- **Real secrets** — a payment provider's secret key, an admin token, anything that can spend money or read other users' data. These never ship. Put the call behind your own backend endpoint, authenticate it with the user's session, and let the server hold the secret.

### Why the usual hiding places do not work
- `--dart-define` and `--dart-define-from-file` values are compiled into the snapshot as constants. They keep the key out of git, not out of the binary.
- A `.env` asset is worse — it is a plain file inside the APK, unzip and read.
- `strings.xml`, `Info.plist` and a hardcoded literal are all one `strings` command away.
- Obfuscation raises the effort a little and protects nothing. Neither does encrypting the key with another key that also ships.

Operationally: assume every shipped key leaks eventually, so make rotation possible without an app update — have the client fetch short-lived credentials from your backend after sign-in. Keep the build-time values in the CI secret store, gitignore the config files, and run a secret scanner on every pull request so the next key does not arrive by commit.

questions.question: How do you set up CI/CD for Flutter with GitHub Actions?
questions.answer:
A Flutter pipeline splits into a CI half that runs on every pull request and a CD half that runs only on protected branches or version tags.

### CI (every PR)
1. Checkout, set up the Flutter SDK, `flutter pub get`
2. `dart format --output=none --set-exit-if-changed .`
3. `flutter analyze --fatal-infos`
4. `flutter test --coverage`
5. Upload coverage and fail the job below your threshold

### CD (merge to main, or a version tag)
1. Build a signed artifact — `.aab` for Play, `.ipa` for the App Store
2. Ship it: Firebase App Distribution / TestFlight for beta, a store track for production

### Things that keep the pipeline from rotting
- Resolve the SDK from `pubspec.yaml` (`flutter-version-file`) instead of hardcoding a version in the workflow — a pinned version nobody bumps is the most common source of "works on my machine".
- iOS jobs need a macOS runner. They are the slowest and priciest lane, so gate them on main/tags rather than every PR, and pick the Xcode version explicitly instead of trusting the image default.
- Keystores, certificates and API keys live in the CI secret store, are decoded into a temp file at build time, and are deleted in an `if: always()` cleanup step. Never commit them.
- Run Dependabot on `.github/workflows` — third-party actions go stale faster than your own code.
questions.code_example:
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
name: Flutter CI

on:
  pull_request:
    branches: [main, develop]
  push:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5

      - uses: subosito/flutter-action@v2
        with:
          # Reads the SDK constraint from pubspec.yaml — no version to bump here
          flutter-version-file: pubspec.yaml
          cache: true

      - run: flutter pub get

      - name: Check formatting
        run: dart format --output=none --set-exit-if-changed .

      - name: Analyze
        run: flutter analyze --fatal-infos

      - name: Test with coverage
        run: flutter test --coverage

      - name: Upload coverage
        uses: codecov/codecov-action@v5
        with:
          files: coverage/lcov.info
          token: ${{ secrets.CODECOV_TOKEN }}   # required for most repos now

  build-android:
    needs: test
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - uses: subosito/flutter-action@v2
        with: { flutter-version-file: pubspec.yaml, cache: true }

      - name: Decode keystore
        run: |
          echo "${{ secrets.KEYSTORE_B64 }}" | base64 --decode > android/app/release.jks

      - name: Build release APK
        env:
          STORE_PASS: ${{ secrets.KEYSTORE_PASS }}
          KEY_ALIAS: ${{ secrets.KEY_ALIAS }}
          KEY_PASS: ${{ secrets.KEY_PASS }}
        run: flutter build apk --release --obfuscate --split-debug-info=symbols/

      - name: Deploy to Firebase App Distribution
        uses: wzieba/Firebase-Distribution-Github-Action@v1
        with:
          appId: ${{ secrets.FIREBASE_APP_ID }}
          # Service-account JSON: `firebase login:ci` tokens are deprecated
          serviceCredentialsFileContent: ${{ secrets.FIREBASE_SA_JSON }}
          groups: beta-testers
          file: build/app/outputs/flutter-apk/app-release.apk
          releaseNotes: "Build from commit ${{ github.sha }}"

      - name: Cleanup signing material
        if: always()
        run: rm -f android/app/release.jks

questions.question: What are Flutter flavors and how do you set up dev/staging/production environments?
questions.answer:
Flavors are build variants compiled from one codebase — the same Dart source shipped as separate, side-by-side installable apps for dev, staging and production.

### What a flavor typically changes
- Application ID / bundle ID, so all three can sit on one device at once
- App name and icon
- API endpoint and feature flags
- Firebase project and analytics destination

Naming differs per platform: Android calls them product flavors (inside a flavor dimension), iOS calls them schemes plus build configurations.

### Setup steps
1. Declare the flavor dimension and `productFlavors` in the app-level Gradle file
2. Add a matching scheme and build configuration per flavor in Xcode
3. Give each flavor a Dart entry point (`lib/main_dev.dart`), or drive everything from `--dart-define`
4. Build with `flutter build apk --flavor dev --target lib/main_dev.dart`

Two things worth knowing. `--dart-define-from-file=config/dev.json` feeds a whole config file in at compile time, which beats a wall of individual `--dart-define` flags and keeps keys out of the repo. And `flutter_flavorizr` generates the Android and iOS boilerplate for you if you would rather not hand-edit Gradle and the Xcode project.

questions.question: How do you sign Android and iOS builds in CI without leaking the keys?
questions.answer:
Signing is the single highest-stakes secret in mobile CI. Lose the upload key and you can't publish updates; leak the .p12 and someone can ship a malicious update under your identity. The discipline is: keys stay encrypted at rest, decoded at build time into a temporary file, and shredded when the job ends.

### Android
- Generate a release keystore (.jks) once, store it Base64-encoded in GitHub Secrets / your CI's secret store
- A keystore.properties file holds storeFile, storePassword, keyAlias, keyPassword — generated on the fly in CI from secrets
- `signingConfigs.release` in build.gradle reads from keystore.properties
- **Use Play App Signing** — let Google hold the upload key. You sign with an upload key, Google re-signs with the actual app signing key. Lose the upload key and you can recover via Play Console.

### iOS
- **Two artifacts**: a Distribution Certificate (.p12) and a Provisioning Profile (.mobileprovision)
- fastlane match is the standard — store both, encrypted, in a private git repo; CI calls `fastlane match appstore --readonly`
- **Alternative**: store .p12 + profile as Base64 in CI secrets, decode in a temp keychain that's deleted after build
- Xcode Cloud sidesteps the whole dance — Apple holds the signing assets and signs the archive for you; the tradeoff is that your build lives in Apple's system, not next to the rest of your CI

### Always
- Mark the secrets as masked in CI output
- Restrict who can read or rotate them; keep an audit log
- Rotate after any team member with access leaves
- Do not commit keystore.properties or .p12 — put them in .gitignore explicitly
questions.code_example:
# .github/workflows/release.yml — Android signing
jobs:
  build-android:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - uses: subosito/flutter-action@v2
        with: { flutter-version-file: pubspec.yaml, cache: true }

      - name: Decode keystore
        run: echo "${{ secrets.KEYSTORE_BASE64 }}" | base64 --decode > android/app/release.jks

      - name: Write keystore.properties
        run: |
          cat > android/key.properties <<EOF
          storeFile=release.jks
          storePassword=${{ secrets.KEYSTORE_PASSWORD }}
          keyAlias=${{ secrets.KEY_ALIAS }}
          keyPassword=${{ secrets.KEY_PASSWORD }}
          EOF

      - name: Build app bundle
        run: flutter build appbundle --release --obfuscate --split-debug-info=symbols/

      - name: Cleanup
        if: always()
        run: |
          rm -f android/app/release.jks android/key.properties

questions.question: How do you manage app versioning in Flutter — version, build number, semver?
questions.answer:
Three numbers travel together in every build: the public version, the build number, and the semantic intent of the change. They serve different audiences.

pubspec.yaml `version` field — `1.4.2+87`:
- `1.4.2` is the public version (semver-style: major.minor.patch). Visible in stores, in About screens.
- `+87` is the build number — strictly increasing integer. Stores require it to be higher than any previously uploaded build.
- Flutter expands this into Android `versionName`/`versionCode` and iOS `CFBundleShortVersionString`/`CFBundleVersion`

### Rules to live by
- Build number must always go up. The cleanest source is the CI build counter (GitHub Actions `${{ github.run_number }}`) or a monotonic timestamp
- Don't let two CI runs produce the same build number — even on a re-run
- Public version follows semver intent: bump patch for fixes, minor for additive features, major for breaking UX/API changes that users care about
- On hotfixes branched from a tagged release, bump only the patch and the build number — don't accidentally release `1.5.0+old` ahead of `1.4.2`

### Driving it from one source
- **Manual**: edit pubspec.yaml on every release. Simple, fragile.
- `flutter build --build-name=1.4.2 --build-number=$RUN_NUMBER` overrides pubspec at build time. Recommended for CI.
- Generated build-info file in code so the running app can show its own version (`PackageInfo.fromPlatform()`).
questions.code_example:
# pubspec.yaml
version: 1.4.2+87
# major.minor.patch+build_number
#  ↓             ↓
#  Android versionName     versionCode = 87
#  iOS CFBundleShortVer    CFBundleVersion

# .github/workflows/release.yml
name: Release
on:
  push:
    tags: ['v*']      # e.g. v1.4.2 triggers a release build

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - uses: subosito/flutter-action@v2
        with: { flutter-version-file: pubspec.yaml, cache: true }

      - name: Derive version
        id: ver
        run: |
          # Strip leading 'v' from the tag
          VERSION="${GITHUB_REF_NAME#v}"
          BUILD="${{ github.run_number }}"
          echo "version=$VERSION"   >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          echo "build=$BUILD"       >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"

      - name: Build (override pubspec values)
        run: |
          flutter build appbundle --release \
            --build-name=${{ steps.ver.outputs.version }} \
            --build-number=${{ steps.ver.outputs.build }} \
            --obfuscate --split-debug-info=symbols/

# ── Read version inside the app at runtime ──────────
# import 'package:package_info_plus/package_info_plus.dart';
#
# final info = await PackageInfo.fromPlatform();
# print('${info.version}+${info.buildNumber}');  // 1.4.2+87

questions.question: How do you automate Play Store and App Store releases from CI?
questions.answer:
Both stores expose APIs for unattended uploads. Reaching them safely from CI is the standard final step of a release pipeline.

### Google Play
- Generate a service account in Google Cloud, grant it Play Console access
- **Download its JSON key** — store as a CI secret
- Use `fastlane supply` or the Gradle `play-publisher` plugin to upload an .aab and bump tracks (internal → alpha → beta → production)
- Tracks let you stage rollouts: upload to internal first, promote when smoke tests pass, then ramp production from 1% → 10% → 100%

### Apple App Store
- Generate an App Store Connect API Key (.p8 + key id + issuer id) — replaces username/password / 2FA pain
- Use `fastlane pilot` to upload to TestFlight, `deliver` to push metadata + binary to App Store, `submit_to_app_review` to start review
- TestFlight build availability typically takes 5–30 minutes after upload
- App Store metadata (screenshots, descriptions, what's new) can be checked into the repo (fastlane metadata) so each release ships with version-controlled copy

### Guardrails
- Always upload to internal/TestFlight first; gate prod promotion on a manual approval step or a green smoke job
- On a build pulled from review, your CI should be able to re-promote a previous artifact rather than rebuild — keep .aab/.ipa artifacts retained for at least 90 days
- Never let a CI matrix accidentally upload the same build to production twice; idempotency check on the build number is cheap insurance
questions.code_example:
# fastlane/Fastfile
default_platform(:android)

platform :android do
  desc 'Upload AAB to Play Console internal track'
  lane :internal do
    upload_to_play_store(
      track: 'internal',
      aab: '../build/app/outputs/bundle/release/app-release.aab',
      json_key_data: ENV['PLAY_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_JSON'],
      release_status: 'completed',
    )
  end

  desc 'Promote internal → production with staged rollout'
  lane :promote do |options|
    upload_to_play_store(
      track: 'internal', track_promote_to: 'production',
      rollout: options[:rollout] || '0.1',  # 10%
      json_key_data: ENV['PLAY_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_JSON'],
    )
  end
end

platform :ios do
  desc 'Upload IPA to TestFlight'
  lane :beta do
    api_key = app_store_connect_api_key(
      key_id: ENV['ASC_KEY_ID'],
      issuer_id: ENV['ASC_ISSUER_ID'],
      key_content: ENV['ASC_API_KEY_P8'],
    )
    upload_to_testflight(
      api_key: api_key,
      ipa: '../build/ios/ipa/Runner.ipa',
      skip_waiting_for_build_processing: true,
    )
  end
end

# .github/workflows/release.yml — release stage
# - run: bundle exec fastlane android internal
# - run: bundle exec fastlane ios beta
# - name: Manual approval for prod ramp
#   uses: trstringer/manual-approval@v1
#   with: { approvers: alice,bob }
# - run: bundle exec fastlane android promote rollout:0.1

questions.question: How do you set up beta distribution with Firebase App Distribution and TestFlight?
questions.answer:
Beta channels are how you get a build into the hands of real users without going through the public store review and ramp. Each platform has a different best-practice channel.

### iOS — TestFlight (Apple-only, no alternative)
- **Internal testers**: up to 100, no review needed, instant access — invite by Apple ID
- **External testers**: up to 10,000, requires Apple's beta review (~24h on first build, automatic on subsequent ones in the same group)
- Build expires after 90 days, so testers always have a fresh artifact
- Crash reports flow into Xcode Organizer / your APM

Android — Firebase App Distribution OR Play Console internal/closed testing:
- **Firebase App Distribution**: by-email invitations, OTA updates, supports APKs (faster turnaround for ad-hoc testing)
- **Play Console internal track**: tied to the store identity — closer to what users actually get; required if you want Play Integrity attestations to work in beta
- **Many teams run both** — Firebase for engineering smoke tests, Play internal for product/QA

### Process hygiene
- Auto-publish every main-branch build to a private internal channel — catches build issues before they touch a tester
- Promote tagged release builds to a wider beta group; keep release notes per build
- Wire crash reports / analytics back to a build\_id so you can correlate beta crashes to commits
- **Have a recovery path**: if a beta is broken, you can roll back testers to an older artifact without going through a full release
questions.code_example:
# .github/workflows/beta.yml
name: Beta
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  android-beta:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - uses: subosito/flutter-action@v2
        with: { flutter-version-file: pubspec.yaml, cache: true }
      - run: flutter build apk --release --obfuscate --split-debug-info=symbols/
      - name: Distribute to Firebase
        uses: wzieba/Firebase-Distribution-Github-Action@v1
        with:
          appId: ${{ secrets.FIREBASE_ANDROID_APP_ID }}
          serviceCredentialsFileContent: ${{ secrets.FIREBASE_SA_JSON }}
          groups: engineering-smoke
          file: build/app/outputs/flutter-apk/app-release.apk
          releaseNotes: |
            Build: ${{ github.sha }}
            Branch: ${{ github.ref_name }}

  ios-testflight:
    runs-on: macos-latest      # Apple silicon since macos-14
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - uses: maxim-lobanov/setup-xcode@v1
        with: { xcode-version: latest-stable }   # never trust the image default
      - uses: subosito/flutter-action@v2
        with: { flutter-version-file: pubspec.yaml, cache: true }
      - name: Build IPA
        run: flutter build ipa --release --obfuscate --split-debug-info=symbols/
      - name: Upload to TestFlight
        run: bundle exec fastlane ios beta
        env:
          ASC_ISSUER_ID: ${{ secrets.ASC_ISSUER_ID }}
          ASC_KEY_ID: ${{ secrets.ASC_KEY_ID }}
          ASC_API_KEY_P8: ${{ secrets.ASC_API_KEY_P8 }}

#       service_credentials_file: 'firebase-cd.json',

#       android_artifact_type: 'APK',

questions.question: How do you avoid flaky integration tests in Flutter CI?
questions.answer:
Integration tests on emulators in CI are notorious for flakes that block green builds for reasons unrelated to your code. The solution is a mix of test design (eliminate timing assumptions) and infra design (eliminate environment surprises).

### Design the tests
- Never `Future.delayed` to wait for UI — use `await tester.pumpAndSettle()` for animations, or pump until a finder appears with a polling helper. Sleeps are the #1 source of flake.
- Replace network with deterministic test doubles. The test should not depend on a real backend, ever. Use a recorded fixture or an in-process fake server (`shelf` works well).
- Stub time. If your code reads `DateTime.now()` or starts timers, expose a Clock abstraction and inject a fake; otherwise tests behave differently at midnight.
- Make IDs stable. Use Keys for finder-by-id rather than text. Translations and rebuilds break text-based finders.
- Reset state between tests. Wipe localStorage/secure storage in setUp; set a fresh ProviderScope (Riverpod) or recreate the Cubits.

### Design the infra
- Use one device per test, not parallel devices on the same emulator — emulators sharing GPU on CI runners stutter
- Boot the emulator with `-no-snapshot-save -no-window -no-boot-anim -gpu swiftshader_indirect` for headless reliability
- **Pre-warm**: open a dummy Flutter app once before running the suite to avoid first-build cold-start variance
- **Quarantine flakes**: tag a test `@Tags(['flaky'])` and run it nightly with retries instead of blocking PRs
- Capture screenshots and logs on failure — re-running blindly hides flake patterns

questions.question: What is fastlane and what does it actually buy you over a hand-rolled CI script?
questions.answer:
fastlane is a Ruby tool that turns the long, error-prone sequences of cert/profile/build/upload commands into named lanes. You write a Fastfile once, then `fastlane release` does the right thing on any machine — local, CI, or a teammate's laptop.

### What lanes wrap
- `match` — synchronizes signing certs and provisioning profiles across the team via an encrypted git repo
- `gym` — builds an iOS .ipa with the right scheme, configuration, export options
- `pilot` / `upload_to_testflight` — uploads to TestFlight and waits for processing
- `supply` / `upload_to_play_store` — uploads .aab/.apk to Play and manages tracks
- `deliver` — manages App Store metadata, screenshots, what's new
- `screengrab` / `snapshot` — automated localized screenshots

### What you actually buy
- **Reproducibility**: any clean machine with the right secrets can produce the same artifact
- **Auditability**: lanes are checked into the repo, code-reviewed like any other code
- **Smaller-blast-radius secrets**: fastlane can use App Store Connect API keys (no human 2FA), match (read-only mode in CI)
- **Recovery patterns**: lanes that re-promote already-built artifacts, lanes that roll back, lanes that bisect a regression by version

### When NOT to bother
- A solo project shipping monthly — bash + `flutter build` \+ a couple of GitHub actions is enough
- If you're already on Bitrise or Codemagic, which abstract this — adding fastlane doubles the layers without much benefit
- On Xcode Cloud, signing, archiving and TestFlight upload are built in; fastlane still earns its place for Play uploads and metadata, but not for the iOS build itself
questions.code_example:
# fastlane/Fastfile
default_platform(:ios)

before_all do
  ensure_git_status_clean
  ensure_git_branch(branch: 'main')
end

platform :ios do
  desc 'Sync signing — read-only in CI'
  lane :certs do
    match(type: 'appstore', readonly: ENV['CI'] == 'true')
  end

  desc 'Build, archive, upload to TestFlight'
  lane :beta do
    certs
    increment_build_number(build_number: ENV['CI_BUILD_NUMBER'] || latest_testflight_build_number + 1)
    build_app(
      scheme: 'Runner',
      export_method: 'app-store',
      output_directory: 'build/ios/ipa',
    )
    upload_to_testflight(
      skip_waiting_for_build_processing: true,
    )
  end

  desc 'Promote latest TestFlight build to App Store, with phased release'
  lane :release do
    deliver(
      submit_for_review: true,
      automatic_release: false,
      phased_release: true,                 # 1% / 2% / 5% / 10% / 20% / 50% / 100%
      force: true,                          # skip metadata HTML preview
      precheck_include_in_app_purchases: true,
      submission_information: { add_id_info_uses_idfa: false },
    )
  end
end

# Usage
# bundle exec fastlane ios beta             # nightly
# bundle exec fastlane ios release          # tagged release
# Override env: ASC_KEY_ID / ASC_ISSUER_ID / ASC_API_KEY_P8 set in CI

questions.question: How do you do staged rollouts and quick rollbacks safely?
questions.answer:
Mobile releases ship to thousands of devices in minutes once you push the button. A staged rollout caps the blast radius if something is broken; a clean rollback path lets you stop bleeding fast.

### Staged rollouts
- **Play Console** — production track supports percentage rollouts (1% → 5% → 20% → 50% → 100%). Bake at each stage for at least 24h while watching crashlytics + key metrics.
- **App Store** — Phased Release ramps 1/2/5/10/20/50/100% over 7 days. You can pause from App Store Connect at any stage.
- Both let you halt and resume. Use the pause button when in doubt — the cost of a 12h delay is negligible.

### What to monitor during a rollout
- Crash-free user rate vs. previous version (set a guardrail: \<0.5% drop is fine, >1% drop pause)
- **Critical funnel metrics**: sign-in success, checkout completion, push opt-in
- Backend errors that spiked with the rollout
- Reviews / support tickets in real time

### Rollback options (in order of preference)
- **Halt the staged rollout** — Play Console immediately stops new users from getting the bad build; Phased Release pauses the ramp
- **Server-side feature flag** — hide the bad feature without an app update. Always ship risky features behind a remote flag.
- Re-release the previous build with a new version number — slow (review queue), but works. Keep the previous artifact warm in CI for 30+ days.
- **Force-update screen** — the app calls a config endpoint that says "please update". The current build still runs but a soft block escalates to hard if needed.

Guardrail: ship every release behind at least one feature flag for the new code paths. "Roll back" by toggling the flag is 1000x faster and safer than re-releasing.
questions.code_example:
# Play Console — staged rollout via fastlane
lane :promote do |opts|
  rollout = opts[:rollout] || '0.05'   # 5% by default
  upload_to_play_store(
    track: 'production',
    track_promote_to: nil,             # already on production from internal
    release_status: 'inProgress',      # required for staged rollouts
    rollout: rollout,
    json_key_data: ENV['PLAY_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_JSON'],
  )
end

# Halt a staged rollout immediately
lane :halt do
  upload_to_play_store(
    track: 'production',
    release_status: 'halted',
    json_key_data: ENV['PLAY_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_JSON'],
  )
end

# ── Server-side feature flag — the fastest "rollback" ──────────
# Firebase Remote Config / GrowthBook / LaunchDarkly. In Dart:
#
#   class FeatureFlags {
#     static Future<bool> get newCheckoutEnabled async {
#       final remote = FirebaseRemoteConfig.instance;
#       await remote.fetchAndActivate();
#       return remote.getBool('checkout_v2_enabled');  // toggle = instant kill
#     }
#   }
#
#   FutureBuilder<bool>(
#     future: FeatureFlags.newCheckoutEnabled,
#     builder: (_, snap) => snap.data == true
#         ? const NewCheckoutFlow()
#         : const LegacyCheckoutFlow(),
#   )

# ── Force-update gate (last resort) ─────────────────────────────
# Server returns: { "min_supported_build": 90 }
# App on build 87 < 90 -> show a blocking screen with a store link.
# Prefer fixing the bug; force-update is an emergency button you rarely press.

questions.question: Every pull request waits 40 minutes on CI. Where does the time actually go in a Flutter pipeline, and what do you cut first?
questions.answer:
Read the per-step timings before changing anything — in almost every slow Flutter pipeline the answer is cold caches plus a macOS runner doing work that a Linux runner could have done.

The four buckets, in the order they usually pay off:

- Caching. Restore the pub cache keyed on `pubspec.lock`, the Gradle caches keyed on the Gradle files plus the lockfile, and the CocoaPods cache keyed on `Podfile.lock`; cache the Flutter SDK itself as well. A key that includes the branch name, or one with no fallback restore key, is a cache that always misses — check the hit rate rather than assuming.

- Lane separation. Format, analyze and unit tests belong on a Linux runner and should run on every PR. Building the two platform artifacts is slow and, on hosted macOS, roughly ten times the price per minute — gate it on main, on tags, or behind a label. Nobody needs an IPA to review a copy change.

- Parallelism. Run the jobs as a matrix rather than one long script, shard the unit suite with `--total-shards` and `--shard-index`, and keep integration and golden tests in their own jobs so a flake there does not block a lint fix.

- Waste. Do not run `flutter clean` in CI — it throws away exactly what you just cached. Do not run `pub get` twice. Run code generation only when its inputs changed. Put format and analyze before the long build so a missing comma fails in 90 seconds, and add a concurrency group that cancels superseded runs on the same branch.

Measure again afterwards. A bigger runner for the iOS lane is often cheaper than the engineering hours spent waiting for a small one.
questions.code_example:
name: ci
on: [pull_request, push]

concurrency:                        # cancel superseded runs on the same ref
  group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

jobs:
  check:                            # cheap lane, every PR, Linux only
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    strategy:
      matrix:
        shard: [0, 1, 2, 3]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: subosito/flutter-action@v2
        with:
          flutter-version-file: pubspec.yaml   # never hardcode the version
          cache: true                          # caches the SDK itself
      - uses: actions/cache@v4
        with:
          path: ~/.pub-cache
          key: pub-${{ runner.os }}-${{ hashFiles('pubspec.lock') }}
          restore-keys: pub-${{ runner.os }}-
      - run: flutter pub get --enforce-lockfile
      - if: matrix.shard == 0                  # fail fast before anything slow
        run: |
          dart format --output=none --set-exit-if-changed .
          flutter analyze --fatal-infos
      - run: flutter test --total-shards 4 --shard-index ${{ matrix.shard }}

  ios:                              # expensive lane, gated
    if: startsWith(github.ref, 'refs/tags/v')
    runs-on: macos-14
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/cache@v4
        with:
          path: ios/Pods
          key: pods-${{ hashFiles('ios/Podfile.lock') }}
      - run: flutter build ipa --release --obfuscate --split-debug-info=build/symbols

questions.question: Golden tests pass on your Mac and fail on the Linux CI runner with a few pixels of difference. What is going on and how do you make them trustworthy?
questions.answer:
A golden is a rendered image, so it encodes the machine that produced it — its fonts, its text shaping, its engine build — not only your widget.

### Where the pixels come from
- Fonts. The test environment ships no real fonts and falls back to a placeholder face unless you load your own. Load them from the repo, not from the host, or a Mac with your brand font installed will bake different glyphs than a bare container.
- Text layout. Shaping, hinting and antialiasing differ between host platforms, which is exactly the sub-pixel noise you are seeing.
- Engine version. Two Flutter versions can rasterize the same widget slightly differently, so an unpinned SDK produces unexplainable diffs.
- Everything the test leaves implicit: device pixel ratio, surface size, locale, theme, and the target platform override.

### Make them deterministic instead of tolerant
1. Pick one platform as the source of truth — the container CI already runs — and generate goldens only there, through the same pinned Flutter image.
2. Load the app's fonts and set the surface size once in `flutter_test_config.dart` so every test in the tree starts identical.
3. Tag golden tests and exclude the tag from the default local run, so developers are not blocked by a diff they cannot legitimately regenerate.
4. Upload the `failures/` directory as a CI artifact — a reviewer needs to see the master, the test image and the diff before deciding.
5. Only then consider a comparator with a small tolerance. A threshold buys quiet at the price of hiding the exact regression goldens exist to catch, so it is a last resort, not the fix.

The rule to state out loud: never commit a golden produced on a laptop when CI verifies on Linux.

questions.question: Production is broken and the fix is three lines of Dart. What are your options for shipping it today?
questions.answer:
Rank the options by how much of the release pipeline each one skips, because the fastest fixes never involve a new binary at all.

1. Flip a flag. If the broken path is behind a remote flag or a kill switch, disabling it is live in seconds with no build, no review and no rollout. This is the entire reason risky features ship behind flags.
2. Fix it on the server. A response the client can no longer choke on is often a smaller change than the client fix, and it reaches every installed version at once.
3. Halt the rollout. Stopping a staged rollout or pausing a phased release does not help users who already have the bad build, but it stops the blast radius from growing while you work.
4. Push a Dart patch over the air. A code-push tool such as Shorebird uploads a patch against a specific release and installed apps pick it up on launch. Two constraints decide whether it is available to you: the release has to have been built through the tool in the first place, so it is a decision you make in calm times, and a patch can only carry compiled Dart. A change to native code, to a plugin's platform side, or to the Flutter version needs a real build. Store rules allow over-the-air fixes that keep the app's primary purpose intact; shipping a whole new feature this way to dodge review is a policy violation.
5. Ship a real release and ask for expedited review. Apple grants expedited reviews for genuine breakage, and Play review is usually hours — with a forced-update gate in the app as the backstop for users who never update.

What makes any of this possible is preparation: flags around risky code, a version gate the app checks at launch, staged rollouts with a crash-free-rate guardrail, and the previous artifact kept warm so you can re-promote instead of rebuild.
questions.code_example:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

# 1) Kill switch — no build, no review, effective immediately
curl -sS -X PATCH "$CONFIG_API/flags/new_checkout" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $CONFIG_TOKEN" \
  -d '{"enabled": false, "reason": "INC-4821 checkout crash"}'

# 2) Stop the bleed: halt the Play staged rollout / pause the phased release
#    (Play Console -> Release -> Halt rollout; App Store Connect -> Pause)
fastlane run google_play_track_version_codes track:production

# 3) Dart-only patch over the air, against one shipped release
shorebird patch android --release-version 1.4.2+87
shorebird patch ios     --release-version 1.4.2+87
shorebird patches list  --release-version 1.4.2+87   # confirm adoption

# 4) Native code, a plugin update or a Flutter bump cannot ride in a patch —
#    build a real release and request expedited review on iOS
flutter build appbundle --release \
  --build-name 1.4.3 --build-number "$GITHUB_RUN_NUMBER" \
  --obfuscate --split-debug-info=build/symbols/1.4.3
fastlane supply --track internal --aab build/app/outputs/bundle/release/app-release.aab

questions.question: Explain Flutter's three trees: Widget, Element, and RenderObject.
questions.answer:
Flutter keeps three parallel trees so that cheap descriptions can be thrown away and rebuilt constantly while the expensive layout objects survive.

- **Widget tree** — immutable blueprints, the thing you write inside `build()`. Recreated from scratch on every build; lightweight value objects; describes WHAT to show.
- **Element tree** — mutable and long-lived. An Element holds its current widget, owns the State for a StatefulWidget, knows its position in the tree, and performs reconciliation between the old and the new widget subtree. `BuildContext` IS the Element.
- **RenderObject tree** — layout, painting and hit testing. Expensive to allocate, so the framework tries hard to update one in place rather than replace it.

Reconciliation rule: at the same position, if the new widget has the same `runtimeType` and the same key, the Element is reused and simply given the new widget (the fast path, and the reason `const` widgets are free). A different type or a different key unmounts the old Element and mounts a new one, which also builds a new RenderObject and drops any State it held.

Keys exist for the cases where matching by position is wrong — reordering, inserting or removing items in a list of stateful children. A `ValueKey` tied to your model id makes Flutter match by identity instead of index, so state, scroll position and animations follow the right item.

questions.question: How does Flutter's rendering pipeline work? Explain the frame lifecycle.
questions.answer:
Every frame runs the same fixed sequence, and the whole sequence has to fit inside one display refresh — roughly 16 ms at 60 Hz, and only 8 ms on a 120 Hz ProMotion screen.

1. Vsync — the display asks for a frame and the Scheduler wakes up
2. Animation tick — tickers and AnimationControllers advance, then post-frame callbacks are queued
3. Build — dirty Elements run `build()` and the new widget subtrees are reconciled
4. Layout — RenderObjects compute sizes: constraints go down, sizes come back up, the parent sets each child's position
5. Compositing bits — the framework works out which subtrees need their own layer
6. Paint — RenderObjects record paint commands into layers; this produces a display list, not pixels
7. Compositing — the layer tree is flattened into a scene and handed to the engine
8. Rasterization — the raster thread turns the scene into pixels

### Two threads, two kinds of jank
- UI thread (Dart) — steps 2 to 7. A red bar here means build or layout is too expensive: too many rebuilds, an unbounded `ListView`, heavy work in `build()`.
- **Raster thread** — step 8. A red bar here means painting is too expensive: shader warm-up, oversized images, too many `saveLayer` calls from `Opacity` and clips.

Impeller is the default rasterizer on iOS and Android and precompiles its shaders, which is what removed the old first-run shader jank; Skia lives on behind the web renderers. DevTools shows the two threads as separate bars, and that split is how you tell "my build is slow" from "my painting is slow".

questions.question: What are slivers in Flutter and how do you build custom scroll effects?
questions.answer:
Slivers are scroll-aware render objects — they know their scroll offset and can change size/appearance as the user scrolls. They're the building blocks of CustomScrollView.

Why slivers?
- Mix different scroll behaviors (collapsing header + list + grid) in one scroll view
- **Efficient** — only render what's visible
- **Enable advanced effects**: parallax, sticky headers, collapsing toolbars

### Built-in slivers
- **SliverAppBar** — collapsing/floating/pinned app bar
- **SliverList / SliverFixedExtentList** — lazy list
- **SliverGrid** — lazy grid
- **SliverToBoxAdapter** — embed any widget
- SliverPadding, SliverFillRemaining, SliverPersistentHeader

Custom slivers with SliverPersistentHeader for sticky section headers.

questions.question: What is BuildContext and what does it actually hold?
questions.answer:
BuildContext is a handle to a location in the Element tree. Each Element implements BuildContext — when you receive `BuildContext context` in `build()`, it IS the Element. The framework hides the cast so you can't accidentally call lifecycle methods, but the identity is real.

### What it knows
- Its position in the tree — parent, ancestor types, depth
- How to walk up to find inherited widgets (`dependOnInheritedWidgetOfExactType`)
- Whether the widget is still mounted
- Theme.of, MediaQuery.of, Scaffold.of, Navigator.of all use it for ancestor lookup

### What it does NOT know
- Anything about descendants by default (no `findChild`)
- Anything about other branches of the tree
- **Its own future** — you cannot pre-compute results that depend on a context that doesn't exist yet

### Lifecycle pitfalls
- A context is valid only while the widget is mounted. After an `await`, you must check `if (!context.mounted)` before using it (or capture what you need from context BEFORE the await).
- Storing a context in a long-lived field is almost always a bug — the underlying Element may be unmounted before you use the context again.
- Using the wrong context for `showDialog` (e.g. capturing context from outside the navigator subtree) leads to dialogs appearing in the wrong route.

questions.question: What are BuildOwner and PipelineOwner, and why split them?
questions.answer:
Flutter splits every frame into two stages with two different owners, because reconciling widgets and laying out render objects have completely different cost profiles and ordering rules.

BuildOwner — owns the Element tree. Responsibilities:
- Track "dirty" elements (those whose widget changed or whose State called setState)
- During the build phase, run buildScope: walk dirty elements in tree order, call build(), reconcile children
- Handle GlobalKey reservations and re-parenting

PipelineOwner — owns the RenderObject tree. Responsibilities:
- Track the "needs-layout", "needs-compositing-bits", "needs-paint" and "needs-semantics" sets
- Each frame, flush each phase in order: flushLayout → flushCompositingBits → flushPaint → flushSemantics
- Enforce the invariants between phases (you cannot paint until layout has settled)

### Why split
- Build is a diff stage — nearly free when nothing changed, and it recurses deeply
- Layout and paint touch heavy native objects with strict ordering rules
- Decoupling lets the framework reuse the Element/Render protocol in other contexts (golden tests, headless rendering, custom embedders)

Most developers never touch these directly — but knowing them explains why setState marks an Element dirty (BuildOwner.scheduleBuildFor) while a RenderObject change like `markNeedsLayout` takes an independent path (PipelineOwner.requestVisualUpdate). Both end up calling scheduleFrame on the Scheduler, which runs both owners on the next vsync.

questions.question: How does compositing work? When does Flutter create a new layer?
questions.answer:
After paint, RenderObjects produce a Layer tree — not a flat bitmap. The compositor (Impeller on iOS and Android, Skia behind the web renderers) walks the layer tree and produces the final scene. Layers exist so that scrolling/animating subtrees can be re-composited without being re-painted.

### What creates a new layer
- `RepaintBoundary` — explicit. Always creates an OffsetLayer; everything inside is composed as a single layer.
- `Opacity` (with values strictly between 0 and 1) — saveLayer + alpha-blend → expensive new layer
- `BackdropFilter` — needs to read the framebuffer behind it → ImageFilterLayer
- `ShaderMask`, `Transform` (3D only), some `ColorFilter` cases
- Animations using `FadeTransition` / `SlideTransition` — they wrap the child in lightweight layers internally
- ClipPath / ClipRRect with antialiasing in some cases

### What does NOT create a layer
- Plain `Container`, `Padding`, `Align`, `SizedBox` — they paint directly into the parent's layer
- An alpha colour on a paint (`Colors.black.withValues(alpha: 0.6)`, which replaced the deprecated `withOpacity`) — shader-level alpha, no extra layer
- `Transform.translate(Offset)` — purely 2D, often a single Matrix4 applied at composite time

### Why it matters
- Each layer is a memory allocation; too many small layers cost RAM and indirection
- A repainted layer doesn't force re-paint of siblings; an unwrapped expensive widget under a sibling that animates DOES
- `RepaintBoundary` is the lever you reach for when DevTools shows a static subtree being repainted because of a neighbor's animation

Debug visibility: `debugPaintLayerBordersEnabled = true;` outlines every layer; `debugRepaintRainbowEnabled = true;` flashes layers on repaint — use both when diagnosing.

questions.question: How does hit testing work in Flutter?
questions.answer:
When the user taps the screen, Flutter walks the RenderObject tree to figure out who consumes the event. That walk is called hit testing.

### The protocol
1. Pointer event lands at coordinates (x, y) in screen space
2. The framework calls `RenderView.hitTest(result, position)` — the root render object
3. Each RenderObject in the path implements `hitTest(BoxHitTestResult result, {Offset position})`:
  - It first asks each child whether they were hit (`hitTestChildren`)
  - Then decides whether IT was hit (`hitTestSelf`)
  - If yes, it adds itself to the result list
4. The result is an ordered list from leaf (deepest, hit-tested first) to root
5. The framework dispatches the event to listeners on each entry — the closest one usually wins (handled events bubble up by convention, but Flutter doesn't auto-bubble — gestures cooperate via the gesture arena)

### Key quirks
- Render boxes outside their parent's bounds are NOT hit-tested — `Stack` with overflow visible can render but not receive events past parent edges. Wrap in `MouseRegion`/`Listener` only inside the parent's clipped area, or restructure.
- Transparent areas of widgets normally don't catch hits. `IgnorePointer` blocks all hits below it; `AbsorbPointer` catches them but doesn't dispatch.
- `GestureDetector` with `behavior: HitTestBehavior.translucent` makes a transparent area still hit-testable — useful for tap-on-empty-space.
- `HitTestBehavior.opaque` blocks descendants from being hit-tested in the same area.
